Rearranging Changes the Sum

What happens to the sum when we reorder a conditionally convergent series?

Positive terms and negative terms both pile up without end. So choosing which side to draw from first pushes the sum around. Nothing like this happens when the absolute series converges.

For example, think of putting 💰 coins into a 🐷 piggy bank and taking them out. If both piles of coins are endless, the order alone changes the balance.

Explain at idea level why rearranging an absolutely convergent series never changes its sum. (Idea level; proof omitted.)

Show hint

  1. If ∑an\sum a_n∑an​ converges absolutely, then for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 there is an NNN with tail ∑n>N∣an∣<ε\sum_{n>N}|a_n| < \varepsilon∑n>N​∣an​∣<ε. (Sketch only; rigorous proof omitted)

  2. A rearrangement's partial sums eventually contain the first NNN terms of the original, so the two partial sums differ only by tail terms — less than 2ε2\varepsilon2ε.

  3. Since ε\varepsilonε is arbitrary, the two sums agree: when tails can be made arbitrarily small, reordering cannot change the sum.
